claims.claim: Deontology (from Greek deon, duty, and logos, study) evaluates the moral rightness of an action by whether it conforms to moral norms or rules the agent has a duty to follow, not solely by its consequences.
Kant argued that the only thing good without qualification is a good will: a will committed to doing what morality requires, which is good in itself and not in virtue of what it achieves or produces.

In Kant's view an action has moral worth only when it is done from duty; an action that merely conforms to duty while motivated by self-interest, self-preservation, sympathy, or happiness does not express a good will.

Kant distinguished hypothetical imperatives, which command conditionally given an end the agent wills, from the categorical imperative, which commands unconditionally for all rational agents regardless of their desires.

The universal law formulation of the categorical imperative instructs agents to act only on maxims they can at the same time will as universal law (Groundwork 4:421); a maxim that cannot even be conceived as universal law yields a perfect duty, while one that cannot be rationally willed yields an imperfect duty.

The humanity formulation of the categorical imperative requires treating humanity, in oneself and in others, always as an end and never merely as a means (Groundwork 4:429); it forbids using persons as mere instruments, not all cooperation with them, since cooperation a person could rationally consent to is permitted.

Consequentialist theories such as utilitarianism hold that an action is right when it produces the greatest good for everyone affected; Kantian deontology is standardly classified as denying this teleological priority, treating rightness as grounded in conformity to duty rather than in the value of outcomes.

Defenders of deontology commonly claim it protects individual rights and dignity (persons are not to be sacrificed merely for good results) and secures consistency (the universal law formulation gives no one a license to make an exception of herself).

A standard objection is that duties can conflict: two rules can apply to one situation (e.g., truthfulness versus protecting someone from harm), and critics argue rule-based ethics lacks a clear procedure for such cases; Ross's pluralist deontology responds by treating duties as prima facie and weighing them to identify the actual duty.

A further standard objection, rigorism, charges that treating moral rules as absolute and admitting no exceptions can be rigid; Ross explicitly criticized Kant on this ground, while defenders argue Kant's rules are grounded in rational willing rather than in rules as brute facts. Relatedly, some critics charge rule worship—devotion to rules for their own sake—which defenders contest.

Ross identified five prima facie duties (fidelity, reparation, gratitude, promoting maximum aggregate good, and non-maleficence) and held that one's actual duty is the action with the greatest balance of prima facie rightness over prima facie wrongness.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether acting from duty is compatible with acting from sympathy, love, or friendship.
positions: Critics object that Kant's account seems to deny moral worth to actions done from emotional concern for others, which many people would rank higher than cold duty.

Defenders reply that Kant's point concerns which consideration is decisive in deliberation: a good will treats duty as sufficient reason for action, which is compatible with having and even cultivating feelings.
SEP reports that controversy persists on this point.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Lesson presents the claim as Kant's position, flags it as controversial, and reports both the criticism and the defenders' response without endorsing either.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether the categorical imperative is genuinely non-consequentialist.
positions: The received reading classifies Kant as deontological because rightness is not grounded in the value of outcomes.

Mill and later theorists such as Hare have argued the universal law formulation can be read as a test of the consequences of universal adoption, with Hare calling the CI 'simply utilitarianism put into other words.'
SEP treats this as a contested reading within the literature.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Lesson adopts the standard deontological reading while noting it is a reading, and references consequentialism only for contrast.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether moral rules admit exceptions (rigorism and rule worship).
positions: Kant's perfect duties admit no exception in favor of inclination, which critics (notably Ross) regard as implausibly rigid.

Ross holds that moral rules are prima facie and never absolute; Kantian defenders argue the theory has resources for handling apparent conflicts and that grounding rules in rational willing answers the rule-worship charge.
Business-ethics commentary notes that unconditional ethics is a recognized challenge when applied to real organizations.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Lesson presents rigorism and rule worship as objections with replies, explicitly marked as objections in an ongoing debate rather than verdicts.
